query: AP hantavirus cruise ship latest May 2026 confirmed
answer: In May 2026, a hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship resulted in three deaths and eight confirmed cases. The ship continued to Spain's Canary Islands after evacuating patients. The risk to the global population remains low.

Title: The Latest: Cruise ship with deadly hantavirus outbreak sails for Spanish islands
# The Latest: Cruise ship with deadly hantavirus outbreak sails for Spanish islands. Health workers in protective gear evacuate patients from the MV Hondius cruise ship into an ambulance at a port in Praia, Cape Verde, Wednesday, May 6, 2026. **PRAIA** – Three cruise ship passengers with suspected hantavirus infections were flown to the Netherlands for treatment Wednesday. Three people have died, and the World Health Organization says there are eight cases, five of them confirmed by laboratory testing. About 150 passengers are isolating in their cabins aboard the Dutch ship at the center of the outbreak. The MV Hondius evacuated the patients via the Cape Verde islands off West Africa, before departing for Spain’s Canary Islands on Wednesday afternoon. The WHO says the risk to the global population from this outbreak is low, with the organization’s top epidemic expert telling The Associated Press, “This is not the next COVID.”. The Argentine government’s leading hypothesis is that a Dutch couple contracted the virus during a bird-watching outing at a garbage dump before boarding the cruise, according to two officials. The cruise ship operator had said two of the passengers who were evacuated “remain in a serious condition.” The third has no symptoms but was “closely associated” with a passenger who died May 2. A German passenger’s body will be taken to Spain’s Canary Islands, where the cruise ship is set to be received, a World Health Organization official told the AP on Wednesday. A plane evacuating two of the patients with suspected hantavirus infections from the cruise ship off Cape Verde is stopping at an airport in the Canary Islands to refuel, the Spanish health ministry said. The World Health Organization’s top epidemic expert told the AP that the risk to the public is low, and the Andes type of the hantavirus is known — even if the WHO has never seen a hantavirus outbreak on a ship. In Germany, the Düsseldorf University Clinic said that one of the three passengers who was evacuated from the ship and is being flown to the Netherlands, who was in contact with one of the hantavirus cases on board the ship, would be brought to the hospital for testing later Wednesday.

results.title: 2026 Multi-country Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship
results.content:
## Background

On May 2, 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of a cluster of severe acute respiratory illness (SARI) among passengers and crew of a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean. The cluster included two deaths and one critically ill passenger, whose laboratory tests confirmed hantavirus. On May 6, 2026, WHO confirmed that the type of hantavirus responsible for this outbreak is the Andes virus. As of May 8, 2026, WHO has reported eight cases (six confirmed and two suspected), including three deaths. Investigations are ongoing to assess exposure risk of all Americans passengers on the cruise ship or who may have been exposed to an infected cruise ship passenger on an aircraft. [...] CDC is working with partners (federal government, state and local and international) on safely repatriating American passengers from the cruise ship to a facility in Nebraska with specialized medical capabilities. On May 7, 2026, CDC sent a team to meet the cruise ship in the Canary Islands, Spain following travel from Cape Verde. The team is prepared to assess exposure risk among U.S. passengers and determine appropriate monitoring measures. [...] May 8, 2026

CDCHAN-00528

CDC Health Advisory

## Summary

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is issuing this Health Alert Network (HAN) Health Advisory to inform clinicians and health departments about a new cluster of hantavirus disease cases caused by infection with Andes virus. Hantavirus disease can cause severe illness and can be fatal. Clinicians should be aware of the potential for imported cases, although the risk of broad spread to the United States is considered extremely unlikely at this time. As a precaution, this Health Advisory summarizes CDC's recommendations for U.S. public health departments, clinical laboratories, and healthcare workers about hantavirus disease case identiﬁcation, testing, and biosafety considerations in clinical laboratories.

PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Three cruise ship passengers with suspected hantavirus infections were flown to the Netherlands on Wednesday for treatment. Three people have died and one body is still on the Dutch ship at the center of the outbreak, the MV Hondius, which is now heading for Spain’s Canary Islands. The patients were evacuated via the Cape Verde islands off West Africa. About 150 passengers are isolating in their cabins, and officials say those on board show no symptoms. The Argentine government’s leading hypothesis is that a Dutch couple contracted the virus during a bird-watching tour at a garbage dump before boarding the cruise, according to two officials. Symptoms of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome usually show between one to six weeks, or more, after contact with an infected rodent. Argentina’s Ministry of Health says it’s working with authorities across the country to retrace the winding path of the Dutch couple that became the first to fall ill with hantavirus on the cruise ship before dying. A plane evacuating two of the patients with suspected hantavirus infections from the cruise ship off Cape Verde is stopping at an airport in the Canary Islands to refuel, the Spanish health ministry said. In Germany, the Düsseldorf University Clinic said that one of the three passengers who was evacuated from the ship and is being flown to the Netherlands, who was in contact with one of the hantavirus cases on board the ship, would be brought to the hospital for testing later Wednesday.

# The Latest: WHO zeros in on cruise ship hantavirus cluster as passengers still stuck on board. Health workers in protective gear evacuate patients from the MV Hondius cruise ship into an ambulance at a port in Praia, Cape Verde, Wednesday, May 6, 2026. PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Three cruise ship passengers with suspected hantavirus infections were being flown to the Netherlands for treatment Wednesday. Three people have died, and the World Health Organization says there are eight cases, five of them confirmed. The MV Hondius is near the Cape Verde islands off West Africa, waiting to sail to Spain’s Canary Islands. The WHO says the risk to the global population from this outbreak is low, with the organization’s top epidemic expert telling The Associated Press, “This is not the next COVID.”. Ann Lindstrand, the WHO representative in Cape Verde, said in a phone interview that a sample from the third patient evacuated from the ship is still being checked. “So far of all the cases related to this boat, the eight cases, we now have five confirmed with laboratory testing for Andes virus,” she said. Two passengers left the cruise ship in South Africa. A plane evacuating two of the patients with suspected hantavirus infections from the cruise ship off Cape Verde is stopping at an airport in the Canary Islands to refuel, the Spanish health ministry said. Samples taken earlier from the patients now evacuated from the ship were examined and also confirmed to be the Andes type, the World Health Organization said at a briefing Wednesday. The World Health Organization’s top epidemic expert told the AP that the risk to the public is low, and the Andes type of the hantavirus is known — even if the WHO has never seen a hantavirus outbreak on a ship. In Germany, the Düsseldorf University Clinic said that one of the three passengers who was evacuated from the ship and is being flown to the Netherlands, who was in contact with one of the hantavirus cases on board the ship, would be brought to the hospital for testing later Wednesday.

# Hantavirus Outbreak on Cruise Ship: Human-to-Human Transmission Confirmed? **The Hantavirus Cruise Ship Outbreak: A Wake-Up Call for Global Health Security**. The recent hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship has captured headlines, but what’s truly alarming isn’t just the outbreak itself—it’s the unexpected twist of potential human-to-human transmission. Hantavirus, traditionally associated with rodent-to-human contact, has now raised questions about its ability to spread among people. Personally, I think this development is a stark reminder of how quickly our understanding of pathogens can evolve, and how vulnerable we remain to the unpredictability of infectious diseases. **What Makes This Outbreak Particularly Troubling?**. With a mortality rate of roughly one-third for those who develop hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), this isn’t your average viral outbreak. What many people don’t realize is that the Andes virus, the suspected culprit here, has historically been confined to South America, primarily spreading through rodent exposure. The idea that it might now be jumping between humans—even in close, prolonged contact—is a game-changer. From my perspective, the cruise ship setting amplifies the concern. The fact that the outbreak started in early April but only gained attention in May highlights the lag in detection and response. If you take a step back and think about it, this isn’t just about a ship; it’s a microcosm of how quickly a localized outbreak can spiral into a global health concern. The WHO’s assurance that the risk to the general public remains low is reassuring, but it shouldn’t lull us into complacency. What makes this particularly fascinating is how it mirrors broader trends in infectious disease outbreaks—think Ebola, Zika, or even COVID-19. In my opinion, the Hondius outbreak is a wake-up call. If you take a step back and think about it, the next pandemic isn’t a matter of if, but when. The hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius is more than a medical curiosity—it’s a mirror reflecting our strengths and vulnerabilities. From my perspective, the real story here isn’t the virus itself, but our response to it. What this really suggests is that global health security isn’t just about vaccines or treatments; it’s about preparedness, collaboration, and humility in the face of nature’s unpredictability.
